title: DTFT and Frequency Response
description: Ten original questions on the DTFT, periodicity, transform properties, frequency response, phase delay and moving-average filters. Multiple-response scoring is for practice only: +1 per correct selection and -0.5 per incorrect selection, floored at zero.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the discrete-time Fourier transform $X(e^{j omega})$ are correct?

options.content: It is formed by summing $x[n]e^{-j omega n}$ over integer $n$.
It is periodic in $omega$ with period $2pi$.
Its frequency variable is continuous even though time is discrete.
Values outside one period are unrelated to values inside it.

questions.explanation: The DTFT maps an integer-indexed sequence to a continuous, $2pi$-periodic frequency function. Adding $2pi$ to $omega$ leaves every exponential basis term unchanged.

questions.prompt: If $x[n]$ has DTFT $X(e^{j omega})$, what is the DTFT of $x[n-n0]$?

options.content: $e^{-j omega n0}X(e^{j omega})$
$X(e^{j(omega-n0)})$
$n0 X(e^{j omega})$
$X(e^{j omega})$ for every $n0$

questions.explanation: A delay in time multiplies the spectrum by a linear-phase factor. Its magnitude is one, so the shift changes phase but not the magnitude spectrum.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 2, DTFT time-shift property

questions.prompt: For $y[n]=x[n]*h[n]$, which frequency-domain statements are correct?

options.content: $Y(e^{j omega})=X(e^{j omega})H(e^{j omega})$.
Where the transforms are nonzero, output phase is input phase plus system phase modulo $2pi$.
Linear convolution in time becomes addition in frequency.

questions.explanation: The convolution theorem turns time-domain convolution into frequency-domain multiplication. Magnitudes multiply and phases add, which makes the frequency response a direct description of how an LTI system modifies each frequency.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 2, convolution and DTFT property

questions.prompt: If $x[n]$ is real-valued, which symmetries hold for its DTFT?

options.content: $X(e^{-j omega})$ is the complex conjugate of $X(e^{j omega})$.
The magnitude spectrum is even in frequency.
The phase is odd where a consistent phase representation is defined.
The DTFT must be purely real at every frequency.

questions.explanation: A real sequence has conjugate-symmetric spectrum. This makes magnitude even and phase odd up to phase wrapping and zeros. The spectrum can still be complex away from special frequencies.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 2, DTFT symmetry properties

questions.prompt: For $x[n]=a^n u[n]$ with $|a|<1$, which expression is its DTFT?

options.content: $1/(1-ae^{-j omega})$
$1-ae^{-j omega}$
$1/(1+ae^{-j omega})$
$delta[omega-a]$

questions.explanation: The transform is the convergent geometric series with ratio $ae^{-j omega}$: its sum is $1/(1-ae^{-j omega})$ when $|a|<1$.

questions.prompt: Because the DTFT is $2pi$-periodic, the inverse DTFT may integrate over any continuous frequency interval of length $2pi$.

options.content: True
False

questions.explanation: One complete period contains all distinct DTFT information. The inverse integral commonly uses $[-pi,pi]$, but any interval of length $2pi$ gives the same sequence.

questions.prompt: A complex exponential $x[n]=e^{j omega0 n}$ is applied to an LTI system with frequency response $H(e^{j omega})$. What follows?

options.content: The output has the same frequency $omega0$.
The complex amplitude is multiplied by $H(e^{j omega0})$.
Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems.
A linear time-invariant system must create unrelated new frequencies from this input.

questions.explanation: The output is $H(e^{j omega0})e^{j omega0 n}$. The system changes magnitude and phase but preserves the exponential's frequency, which is precisely the eigenfunction property.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 2, frequency response interpretation

questions.prompt: An LTI system has an absolutely summable impulse response. Which statements follow?

options.content: The system is BIBO stable.
Its frequency response exists as a bounded continuous function.
$|H(e^{j omega})|$ is bounded by the absolute sum of $h[n]$.
Absolute summability alone proves the system is causal.

questions.explanation: Absolute summability is the LTI BIBO-stability condition and guarantees convergence and boundedness of the DTFT. Causality is separate and requires $h[n]=0$ for negative $n$.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 2 Tutorial, stability and DTFT questions

questions.prompt: What qualitative frequency response is expected from a finite moving-average filter with equal positive coefficients?

options.content: It passes or preserves the DC component after suitable normalization.
It smooths rapid sample-to-sample variation.
Its main behaviour is low-pass.
Its magnitude is exactly one at every frequency.

questions.explanation: Averaging reinforces slowly varying components and suppresses many high-frequency variations. Normalized equal coefficients sum to one, giving unit gain at DC, but the response is not flat across all frequencies.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 2 Tutorial, moving-average filter

questions.prompt: Why is a linear phase response often desirable in a filter passband?

options.content: Frequency components experience a common time delay.
The waveform shape is preserved when magnitude distortion is also controlled.
The phase has the form $-omega D$ plus a constant over the relevant band.
Linear phase always means zero delay.

questions.explanation: A phase proportional to frequency corresponds to a time shift $D$. Equal delay across frequency avoids phase distortion, though the delay need not be zero and the magnitude response can still alter amplitudes.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 3, phase distortion and delay, slides 7-9
